sections.heading: C — Intersections, right-of-way, turning, roundabouts and special interchanges
sections.markdown:
## C — Intersections, right-of-way, turning, roundabouts and special interchanges

FACT_ID: sec09-F01 | anchor: A121
An intersection is any spot where two or more roads meet, including cross streets, roundabouts, calming circles, side streets, driveways and shopping center or parking lot entrances. [A121]
Source: [A121 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec09-F02 | anchor: A121
Every intersection is legally a crosswalk, whether or not a crosswalk is painted. [A121]
Why it matters: you yield to a walker at a corner even when no lines are painted there.
Source: [A121 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec09-F03 | anchor: A121
Before entering an intersection, yield to pedestrians and traffic already in it, look each way more than once, and check mirrors and over your shoulder for cyclists, motorcyclists or walkers entering your path. [A121]
Source: [A121 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec09-F04 | anchor: A121
If your view of the cross street is blocked after stopping at the stop line, creep forward slowly until you can see, which also lets crossing drivers spot your front end first. [A121]
Source: [A121 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec09-F05 | anchor: A122
Do not start across or into a turn unless there is room to finish without blocking the intersection. [A122]
Source: [A122 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0122]

FACT_ID: sec09-F06 | anchor: A122
Scan the whole area around an intersection with extra care near shopping centers, parking lots, construction, busy sidewalks, playgrounds, parks and schoolyards. [A122]
Source: [A122 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0122]

FACT_ID: sec09-F07 | anchor: A122
Right-of-way rules set the order in which vehicles move through an intersection, and the law decides who must yield, meaning give it up. [A122]
Source: [A122 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0122]

FACT_ID: sec09-F08 | anchor: A122
At a four-way stop, vehicles go in the order they arrived, and when two arrive at about the same time, the driver on the left yields to the one on the right. [A122]
Source: [A122 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0122]

FACT_ID: sec09-F09 | anchor: A122
At a four-way stop, a driver turning left must yield to vehicles going straight or turning right. [A122]
Source: [A122 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0122]

FACT_ID: sec09-F10 | anchor: A122
At a two-way stop, the vehicle going straight has the right-of-way and turning vehicles must yield to it. [A122]
Source: [A122 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0122]

FACT_ID: sec09-F11 | anchor: A123
Washington law requires you to turn, left or right, into the lane nearest the direction you are coming from, and you may change lanes only after finishing the turn. [A123]
Why it matters: swinging wide into a far lane breaks this rule even if that lane is empty.
Source: [A123 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec09-F12 | anchor: A123
With more than one turn lane, stay in the same lane through the whole turn so you never drift into the next lane. [A123]
Source: [A123 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec09-F13 | anchor: A123
Signal at least 100 feet before turning left or right across oncoming traffic, then wait for a safe gap and check that the street you are entering is clear of vehicles, walkers and bicyclists. [A123]
Source: [A123 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec09-F14 | anchor: A123
Check behind you for bicyclists and yield to them before you turn, since they may be closing on you faster than you think. [A123]
Source: [A123 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec09-F15 | anchor: A124
In Washington a U-turn is generally legal unless a sign forbids it, but you need clear sight in every direction, so never make one on a curve or near the top of a hill. [A124]
Source: [A124 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec09-F16 | anchor: A124
A four-way junction carrying at least one lane in each direction is called a cross intersection; it may be controlled by lights, signs or markings, and you apply the right-of-way laws there. [A124]
Source: [A124 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec09-F17 | anchor: A124
A T-intersection is a three-way junction where one road ends at a through road, and a yield or stop sign there shows that through traffic has the right-of-way. [A124]
Source: [A124 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec09-F18 | anchor: A124
At a Y-intersection a minor road joins a major route, often with a stop sign on the minor road, and cars on the major road have the right-of-way. [A124]
Source: [A124 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec09-F19 | anchor: A125
At a mid-block crosswalk, pedestrians in a marked crosswalk always have the right-of-way, and drivers should stop for walkers and bicyclists even with no stop sign. [A125]
Source: [A125 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0125]

FACT_ID: sec09-F20 | anchor: A125
A traffic calming circle has a painted or raised center island that traffic circles counterclockwise, may post stop or yield signs on every approach, a few of them or none, and uses the ordinary right-of-way rules. [A125]
Source: [A125 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0125]

FACT_ID: sec09-F21 | anchor: A125
Calming circles are built for passenger cars, so give fire trucks, buses and delivery trucks room, since they may need to go clockwise around the island. [A125]
Source: [A125 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0125]

FACT_ID: sec09-F22 | anchor: A126
In a roundabout every approaching vehicle yields on entry and then travels counterclockwise around a raised center island, and roundabouts are designed to serve cars, large trucks, buses, bicyclists and pedestrians alike. [A126]
Source: [A126 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec09-F23 | anchor: A127
Large vehicles may drive over a roundabout's truck apron and use both lanes, so give them plenty of space and stay well back from trucks. [A127]
Source: [A127 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec09-F24 | anchor: A127
A bicyclist may ride through a roundabout either as a pedestrian or as a vehicle, and when riding as a vehicle should take the middle of the lane to be seen. [A127]
Source: [A127 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec09-F25 | anchor: A127
Slow down as you approach, because roundabouts are designed for speeds of 15 to 25 mph. [A127]
Source: [A127 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec09-F26 | anchor: A127
Use the lane choice sign to pick your lane for a right turn, going straight or a left turn before you enter, then stay in that lane until you leave the roundabout. [A127]
Source: [A127 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec09-F27 | anchor: A127
Stop for pedestrians and bicyclists in the crosswalks on both entry and exit, look left and yield to all traffic already circulating, then enter to the right going counterclockwise when there is a gap. [A127]
Why it matters: traffic already inside the roundabout has the right-of-way over entering traffic.
Source: [A127 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec09-F28 | anchor: A127
If an emergency vehicle approaches while you are in a roundabout, drive on through it and then pull over, as at any other intersection. [A127]
Why it matters: stopping inside the circle is not the move; you clear it first.
Source: [A127 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec09-F29 | anchor: A128
A diverging diamond is a newer Washington interchange that shifts traffic to the opposite side of the road so left turns onto and off freeway ramps flow better, with fewer crossing points and less crash risk. [A128]
Source: [A128 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0128]

FACT_ID: sec09-F30 | anchor: A129
In a diverging diamond, markings and signals guide you to the left side of the road, you turn left onto the freeway without stopping or yielding to oncoming traffic, and you cross back to the right after the overpass or underpass. [A129]
Source: [A129 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec09-F31 | anchor: A129
An uncontrolled intersection has no signs, the normal right-of-way rules still apply, and such intersections are usually on local roads and streets. [A129]
Source: [A129 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec09-F32 | anchor: A129
At an uncontrolled intersection you must yield if a vehicle is already in it, if you are entering or crossing a state highway from a secondary road, if you are moving from an unpaved to a paved road, or if you are turning left with a vehicle coming from the opposite direction. [A129]
Source: [A129 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0129]

Glossary: right-of-way — the order the law gives for moving through an intersection [A122]. Yield — give up the right-of-way [A122]. Truck apron — the strip around a roundabout's center island built for large vehicles [A127]. Diverging diamond — an interchange that briefly moves traffic to the left side for easier left turns [A128]. Uncontrolled intersection — one with no signs [A129].
Memory aid: at a four-way stop think first come, first go, and ties go to the right [A122].
